text: Woe to those who lounge at ease in Zion, and to those who feel secure on Mount Samaria — you notable men of the foremost nation, to whom the house of Israel comes!

versions.text: Woe to those who lounge at ease in Zion, and to those who feel secure on Mount Samaria — the notable men of the foremost of nations, to whom the house of Israel comes.
versions.explanation: "The foremost of nations" is a stacked genitive that stumbles when read aloud; "the foremost nation" carries the same sense more smoothly, and the direct address better fits the accusatory tone of the woe.

text: Cross over to Calneh and look; go on from there to great Hamath, then down to Gath of the Philistines. Are they better than these kingdoms of yours? Is their territory greater than yours?

versions.text: Cross over to Calneh and look; go on from there to great Hamath, then down to Gath of the Philistines. Were they better than these kingdoms? Was their territory greater than yours?
versions.explanation: "These kingdoms" is ambiguous in English — a hearer will most naturally take it to refer to the cities just named, whereas the Hebrew contrasts them with Israel and Judah. Adding "of yours" matches the following "than yours" and clarifies the comparison for oral reading.

text: You push away the day of disaster, yet you bring the reign of violence near.
You lie on beds inlaid with ivory and sprawl on your couches; you eat lambs from the flock and calves from the fattening stall.
You improvise to the sound of the harp and, like David, invent instruments for your songs.
You drink wine by the bowlful and anoint yourselves with the finest oils, but you do not grieve over the ruin of Joseph.
Therefore you will be the first to go into exile, and your sprawling revelry will come to an end.
The Lord GOD has sworn by himself — this is the declaration of the LORD, the God of hosts: I detest the pride of Jacob and hate his citadels; I will hand over the city and everything in it.
And if ten men are left in a single house, they too will die.

When a relative — the one who burns the bodies — comes to carry the bones out of the house, he will ask whoever is in the innermost room, "Is anyone else with you?" and the answer will come, "No one." Then he will say, "Silence! The name of the LORD is not to be spoken."
For look, the LORD is giving the command: he will smash the great house to rubble and the small house to pieces.
Do horses gallop over rock? Does anyone plow it with oxen? Yet you have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness.

You rejoice over Lo-debar, saying, "Have we not taken Karnaim by our own strength?" [Footnote: The Hebrew plays on two place names captured by Israel: Lo-debar sounds like "nothing," and Karnaim means "horns," a symbol of strength.]

versions.text: You rejoice over nothing at all, saying, "Have we not taken Karnaim by our own strength?"
versions.explanation: The verse is built on a double wordplay with two captured towns. The translation keeps Karnaim as a place name but renders Lo-debar as "nothing at all," which breaks the parallel and leaves the two halves inconsistent. Either keep both place names with an explanatory footnote, or render both as puns.

text: But look, I am raising up a nation against you, house of Israel — this is the declaration of the LORD, the God of hosts — and they will oppress you from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah.
